questiontext.text: What best describes the core behavior of depth-first search?

answer.text: It goes as deep as possible along a path, then backtracks when it can go no further

feedback.text: Correct — DFS dives deep and backtracks at dead ends.

answer.text: It visits all vertices at distance d before any at distance d+1

feedback.text: That is breadth-first search, not DFS.

answer.text: It repeatedly adds the globally cheapest edge that avoids a cycle

feedback.text: That describes Kruskal's MST algorithm.

answer.text: It grows a tree by adding the minimum crossing edge each step

feedback.text: That describes Prim's MST algorithm.

generalfeedback.text: DFS follows one branch to its end, backtracking whenever the current vertex has no unvisited neighbors.

questiontext.text: An iterative (non-recursive) DFS explicitly manages its frontier with which data structure?

answer.text: A LIFO stack

feedback.text: Correct — a stack reproduces the last-in-first-out order that recursion gives.

answer.text: A FIFO queue

feedback.text: A queue produces breadth-first order, not depth-first.

answer.text: A min-heap keyed by weight

feedback.text: DFS ignores weights; a min-heap belongs to Prim or Dijkstra.

answer.text: A hash map of edge weights

feedback.text: DFS orders vertices by depth, not by any weight map.

generalfeedback.text: Recursion uses the call stack implicitly; an iterative DFS makes that stack explicit to achieve LIFO exploration.

questiontext.text: Using an adjacency list, what is the time complexity of DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges?

answer.text: O(V + E)

feedback.text: Correct — each vertex and edge is processed a constant number of times.

answer.text: O(E log V)

feedback.text: That is Prim/Dijkstra with a heap; DFS needs no priority queue.

answer.text: O(V log V) always

feedback.text: DFS does no sorting; it is linear in V + E.
DFS visits each vertex once, so it is linear, not exponential.

generalfeedback.text: Like BFS, DFS touches every vertex once and scans every edge once, giving O(V + E).

questiontext.text: Which classic task is DFS the natural basis for?

answer.text: Topological sorting of a directed acyclic graph

feedback.text: Correct — finishing times from DFS give a topological order.

answer.text: Computing fewest-edge shortest paths in an unweighted graph

feedback.text: That is BFS's specialty, not DFS.

answer.text: Building a minimum spanning tree greedily by weight

feedback.text: That is Kruskal or Prim, which sort or prioritize by weight.

answer.text: Halving the number of components each round in parallel

feedback.text: That describes Borůvka's MST algorithm.

generalfeedback.text: DFS underpins topological sort, cycle detection, connected components, and strongly connected components (SCC).

questiontext.text: When DFS reaches a vertex whose neighbors are all already visited, it backtracks to the most recent vertex that still has unexplored neighbors.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — backtracking to the latest branching point is exactly how DFS proceeds.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Backtracking at dead ends is the defining mechanic of DFS.

questiontext.text: DFS always finds the path with the fewest edges between two vertices in an unweighted graph.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — DFS may reach a target by a long, deep detour; use BFS for fewest-edge paths.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — DFS gives no shortest-path guarantee; BFS does that for unweighted graphs.

questiontext.text: Aside from recursion, an iterative DFS drives its traversal with an explicit LIFO ______ (single English word).

answer.text: stack

feedback.text: Correct — a LIFO stack mirrors the recursion order.

answer.text: stack*

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about depth-first search are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It runs in O(V + E) with an adjacency list

feedback.text: Yes — linear in vertices plus edges.

answer.text: It can be used to detect cycles and to find connected components

feedback.text: Yes — both are standard DFS applications.

answer.text: It uses a FIFO queue to explore level by level

feedback.text: No — that is BFS; DFS uses a stack/recursion.

answer.text: It guarantees the fewest-edge path in an unweighted graph

feedback.text: No — that guarantee belongs to BFS, not DFS.

generalfeedback.text: DFS is a stack/recursion-based O(V + E) traversal used for cycle detection, components, and topological sort; queue-based level order and fewest-edge shortest paths belong to BFS.
